TABLE OF CONTENTS

I. AEDPA’s Text and Structure Confirm the
Director’s Interpretation. ............................................ 2
A. A rule was previously  available if a prisoner
could have presented a claim relying
on the rule. ............................................................... 2
B. The structure of § 2244(b)(2) confirms the
Director’s interpretation. .................................... 12
C. Atkins was not “previously unavailable” to
Johnson. ................................................................. 16
D. The Director has consistently urged the
adoption of the Eleventh Circuit’s decision in
In re Bowles. ......................................................... 18
II. AEDPA Limits Second or Successive Petitions. .... 21
Conclusion ......................................................................... 23

1
REPLY BRIEF
In AEDPA, Congress created “strict procedural
hurdles” that prisoners must overcome before a federal
court can consider a second or successive habeas filing
on the merits. Rivers v. Guerrero , 605 U.S. 443, 446
(2025); see also Jones  v. Hendrix , 599 U.S. 465, 476
(2023) (“AEDPA strictly limi ted ‘second or successive’
§ 2255 motions[.]”). Section 2244(b)(2)(B)’s limits for
raising a claim based on a newly discovered factual
predicate necessarily mean th at a prisoner may discover
a new factual predicate for a claim but be unable to assert
that claim in a second or successive habeas filing. 28
U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B). In many circumstances, including
those of this case, Congress chose “finality over error
correction.” Jones, 599 U.S. at 480.
Congress had sound reasons for its policy choice. The
Director’s opening brief and the States’ amicus brief
demonstrate the sovereign harm from upsetting finality.
State Amicus Br. 2 (explaining that finality is “essential
to the operation of our crimin al justice system” and that
its absence creates “a profound injury to the powerful
and legitimate interest in punishing the guilty” (citations
and quotation marks omitted)). And the amicus brief of
Mr. Aparece confirms the re al injury that delay and
uncertainty inflict on victim s’ families. Aparece Amicus
Br. 14–16.
The rule of Atkins—that the Constitution prohibits
the execution of the intellect ually disabled—has always
been available to Johnson. He cited Atkins and argued
for an extension of its rule in his initial federal habeas
application over a decade ago. Johnson v. Stephens , 617
F. App’x 293, 303 (5th Ci r. 2015) (per curiam).

2

Rather than a legal development, Johnson’s Atkins
claim relies on a new factual predicate: publication of the
DSM-5. Johnson’s argument th at changes in diagnostic
standards allow the assertion of  this claim in a second or
successive application cannot be harmonized with
AEDPA’s text: a claim resting on a new factual predicate
must pass through the gatewa y of § 2244(b)(2)(B), which
Johnson cannot satisfy.
In balancing finality against error correction,
Congress imposed strict limits  on second or successive
habeas petitions. The judgment below should be
reversed.
ARGUMENT
I. AEDPA’s Text and Structure Confirm the
Director’s Interpretation.
A. A rule was previously av ailable if a prisoner
could have presented a claim relying on the
rule.
1. Johnson correctly acknowle dges that “available”
modifies “rule” in § 2244(b)(2)(A). Resp. Br. 12.
Nonetheless, Johnson effectiv ely equates availability of
a rule with the availability of  a claim relying on the rule,
embracing the Fifth Circuit’s holding. See In re Cathey ,
857 F.3d 221, 232 (5th Cir. 201 7) (per curiam) (reasoning
that “a claim must have some possibility of merit to be
considered available” ). Johnson’s argument fails to give
effect to AEDPA’s textual focu s on the availability of a
“rule.”
Johnson correctly recognizes that a claim comprises
a legal rule and factual predicate. Resp. Br. 19. “[A]
‘claim’ as used in § 2244(b) is an asserted federal basis
for relief from a state court’ s judgment of conviction.”

3

Gonzalez v. Crosby , 545 U.S. 524, 530 (2005). A rule—
without supporting facts or argument—is not “an
asserted federal basis for relief” from a judgment, and as
in this case, a rule can be available to a petitioner, even
in the absence of the factua l predicate necessary for a
claim relying on the rule to succeed.
The parties generally agree on the definition of
“available”: “present or re ady for immediate use.” Resp.
Br. 12 (quoting Available, Black’s Law Dictionary (6th
ed. 1990)); Opening Br. 19 (same definition); see also
Webster’s New World College Dictionary 94 (4th ed.
2002) (“that can be used; usab le”). As the United States
explains, a rule is “‘available’ when it can be invoked as
the basis for a claim for relief,” i.e., after it has been
announced by this Court.  U.S. Amicus Br. 25.
Johnson acknowledges that a carpenter likely has a
hammer “available,” even when working on a task for
which a hammer would not be necessary or useful, but he
notes that a hammer is not available when it is “locked in
a toolbox.” Resp. Br. 13. The Director agrees, but this
example hardly helps Johnson. The rule of Atkins was
not locked away. Johnson co uld have asserted a claim
based on Atkins, and Atkins would have served as a rule
of decision. At most, Johnson can say that he could not
have asserted a successful claim until he was diagnosed
as intellectually disabled. This is the equivalent of
arguing that the absence of a nail makes a hammer
unavailable. But a rule becomes “available” when it is
“capable of use,” not when it is useful. “[C]ompulsory
process” similarly is am ong the “[c]onstitutional
safeguards available to defendants,” Perry v. New
Hampshire, 565 U.S. 228, 237 (2 012), even defendants
who have no witness testimony to present.

4

AEDPA recognizes that ex ternal impediments may
prevent a petitioner from raising a claim. See, e.g. , 28
U.S.C. § 2244(d)(1)(B ) (limitations runs from the date on
which an “impediment to filing . . . is removed, if the
applicant was prevented fr om filing by such State
action”); Shinn v. Ramirez , 596 U.S. 366,  379 (2022)
(cause to overcome procedural default can be shown if
“some objective factor external to the defense impeded
counsel’s efforts to comply”).
But futility—that a claim would have been
unsuccessful—is different from an impediment to filing.
See Engle v. Isaac , 456 U.S. 107, 130 (1982) (“[T]he
futility of presenting an objection to the state courts
cannot alone constitute cause for a failure to object at
trial.”); Bousley v. United States, 523 U.S. 614, 623 (1998)
(rejecting the argument that “default should be excused
because” of futility). Futility of a claim similarly does not
render a rule unavailable. In re Bowles , 935 F.3d 1210,
1218 (11th Cir. 2019) (noting the “flaw” of “equat[ing] the
word ‘cognizable’ with the word ‘meritorious’”).
2. Johnson’s argument that a rule was previously
unavailable to a prisoner if it “was of no practical use,”
Resp. Br. 12, relies on cases under the Prison Litigation
Reform Act (PLRA) that invo lve a different context and
a different object that must be “available.”
Booth v. Churner  addresses the exhaustion
requirement, which prohibits “a n action . . . with respect
to prison conditions under section 1983 . . . until such
administrative remedies as are available are exhausted.”
532 U.S. 731, 736 (2001) (quoti ng 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(a)).
This Court considered whet her a remedial scheme was
available when “the administrative process has authority

5

to take some action in response to a complaint, but not
the remedial action an inmate demands.” Id.
Both parties relied on dictio nary definitions, but this
Court found “this exercise in  isolated definition . . .
ultimately inconclusive”: “[D]epending on where one
looks, ‘remedy’ can mean eith er specific relief obtainable
at the end of a process of seeking redress, or the process
itself, the procedural avenue leading to some relief.” Id.
at 738.1
This Court turned to context to resolve the
ambiguity: “[T]he word ‘exhausted’ has a decidedly
procedural emphasis. It makes sense only in referring to
the procedural means, not the particular relief ordered.”
Id. at 739. “[O]ne ‘exhausts’ processes, not forms of
relief.” Id. Thus, this Court held, an administrative
remedy would be available for purposes of PLRA
exhaustion even if it could no t provide the sp ecific relief
sought by a prisoner. Id. at 741.
In Ross v. Blake , this Court provided examples of
circumstances in which a process, although purportedly
available, was not in fact avai lable. 578 U.S. 632, 643–44
(2016). First, no process is available “when (despite what
regulations or guidance ma terials may promise) [a
process] operates as a simp le dead end—with officers

1 Johnson’s medication example, Resp. Br. 13, illustrates a similar
distinction. If the question is whether a treatment is available, then
access to a medication that could not treat the patient’s condition
would not count. But if the question is whether a specific medication
is available, then it is available if  it is in a cabinet in the bathroom,
regardless of whether any person has any condition that the
medication could treat. Section 2244(b)(2)(A) resemb les the latter,
asking whether a “rule” was previously unavailable, not whether the
petitioner had a viable claim or remedy available.

6

unable or consistently unwillin g to provide any relief to
aggrieved inmates.” Id. at 643. Prisoners might be
directed to submit grievances to an office that “disclaims
the capacity to consider those petitions.” Id. Second, “an
administrative scheme might be so opaque that it
becomes, practically speaking, incapable of use,” id., i.e.,
“so confusing that no reasonable prisoner can use [it],”
id. at 644 (internal quotation marks omitted). Third,
“prison administrators [mig ht] thwart inmates from
taking advantage of a grievance process through
machination, misrepresentat ion, or intimidation.” Id.
Booth and Ross provide minimal guidance in this
case. As Booth illustrates, the meaning of “available”
depends heavily on what must be available. 532 U.S. at
738. Ross’s discussion of the availability of a “process”
under the PLRA’s exhaustion requirements sheds little
light on the meaning of the availability of a “rule” under
AEDPA. Whether a “watercraf t” is “‘capable of being
used’ for maritime transport,” Resp. Br. 15 (quoting
Stewart v. Dutra Constr. Co. , 543 U.S. 481, 494 (2005)),
similarly does not illumi nate whether a “rule” was
“previously unavailable.”
To the extent that Ross provides useful guidance, its
examples of unavailability support the Director. The
examples concern procedural impediments to an
administrative process, not the likely outcome of that
process or whether an administrative claim would have
been meritorious. Ross does not suggest that an
administrative process is un available merely because a
request for relief would have been unsuccessful. See also
Booth, 532 U.S. at 741 n.6 (“[W]e stress the point . . . that
we will not read futility or other exceptions into statutory
exhaustion requirements wh ere Congress has provided

7

otherwise.”). A watercraft is  similarly capable of being
used for maritime transport by a person who has no need
or desire to be transported.
No procedural barriers simi lar to those identified in
Ross prevent prisoners from relying on rules in habeas
petitions. The federal courts  remain open for prisoners
to seek habeas relief.
Johnson has not argued that any procedural
impediment prevented him from asserting a claim
relying on the rule of Atkins. He merely contends that
such a claim would have been unsuccessful—that it
lacked merit—until he received a diagnosis of
intellectual disability unde r the DSM-5. If this Court
looks to Ross, its reasoning confirms  that the rule of
Atkins was available to Johnson.
3. This distinction also an swers Johnson’s argument
(at 17) that the Director’s  position is internally
inconsistent because of hi s arguments regarding this
Court announcing a rule wh ile a habeas petition is
pending.
As an initial matter, this sc enario is not implicated in
this case. The availability of a rule announced while a
habeas petition is pending is irrelevant to Johnson, who
committed his crimes after th is Court’s decision in
Atkins. And if the Court agrees with Johnson that there
is tension in the Director’s position, this Court could
adopt a bright-line rule th at a rule was previously
available if it was announce d before the entry of final

8

judgment in the previous petition. Rivers, 605 U.S. at
453.2
But there is no internal inconsistency in the
interpretation adopted by the Eleventh Circuit and
urged by the Director: “[O]ur feasibility analysis does
not focus on whether the claim would have been a
winning one at the time of the first petition, but on
whether it would have  been feasible for the petitioner to
bring the claim then.” In re Bowles, 935 F.3d at 1219. In
other words, when a rule is announced while a habeas
petition is pending, availabi lity depends on whether the
rule could have served as a rule of decision or whether
there was a procedural barrier to a prisoner invoking it.
This is roughly akin to the procedural impediments
recognized by this Court as rendering an administrative
process unavailable in Ross. In neither circumstance
does availability depend on a claim’s factual predicate.
That the DSM-5 was published while Johnson’s initial
habeas petition was pending is irrelevant. Contra Resp.
Br. 31 (asserting that Johnson prevails under the
Director’s interpretation). Changes in the diagnostic
standards for intellectual disability do not affect whether
a “new rule of constituti onal law” was previously
available to a petitioner. The rule of Atkins has always
been available to Johnson, regardless of when he
possessed the necessary factual predicate to assert a
meritorious Atkins claim.

2 Under Rivers, an amendment of a pending habeas petition to
assert a new ground of relief filed before a district court’s entry of
final judgment does not constitute a second or successive
application. 605 U.S. at 453. But classifying a document actually
filed is different from asking whether a rule was available.

9

4. Johnson contends that the Director’s
interpretation of “previousl y unavailable” renders “new
rule” surplusage. See Resp. Br. 17 (“Every rule that was
announced after the last fede ral habeas litigation would
also, by default, be after th e direct appeal was final. So
the Director’s reading leaves ‘new rule’ without
effect[.]”).
As an initial matter, “[t]he  anti-surplusage canon is
not an iron rule.” Mullin v. Al Otro Lado , 609 U.S. 258,
272 (2026). Though the canon “is useful,” it is
“subordinate to the ‘cardinal canon’ that ‘a legislature
says in a statute what it means and means in a statute
what it says there.’” Id. at 273 (quoting U.S. Postal Serv.
v. Konan, 607 U.S. 391, 406 (2026)).
More significantly, the phrase “new rule of
constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral
review by the Supreme Court, ” refers to this Court’s
retroactivity jurisprudence from Teague v. Lane , 489
U.S. 288, 301 (1989) (plurali ty op.), and its progeny. See
Tyler v. Cain , 533 U.S. 656, 665 (2001) (explaining, in
discussing § 2244(b)(2 )(A), that “[u]nder Teague, a new
rule can be retroactive to cases on collateral review”); see
also Williams v. Taylor , 529 U.S. 362, 380 n.12 (2000)
(non-majority opinion of Stevens, J.) (noting “the
verbatim adoption of the Teague language in”
§ 2244(b)(2)(A) and § 2254(e)(2)).
If Congress had used language other than “new rule”
and “retroactive,” the statute might well have been read
to direct this Court to depart from its existing
retroactivity jurisprudence. And as the United States
notes, the definition of “new  rule” includes substantive
aspects. U.S. Amicus Br. 15–16; see also Teague, 489 U.S.

10

at 301 (“In general, however, a case announces a new rule
when it breaks new ground or imposes a new obligation
on the States or the Fe deral Government.”).
Johnson insists that “A EDPA does not codify
Teague,” Resp. Br. 26 (quoting Rodriguez v.
Superintendent, Ba y State Corr. Ctr. , 139 F.3d 270, 274
(1st Cir. 1998)),3 but this is true in the sense that AEDPA
“eliminates the lower federal courts’ role in deeming new
rules of constitutional law a permissible basis for habeas
relief.” Rodriguez, 139 F.3d at 274–75; see also Tyler, 533
U.S. at 666 (“The most he ca n claim is that, based on the
principles outlined in Teague, this Court should make
Cage retroactive to cases on co llateral review. What is
c l e a r ,  h o w e v e r ,  i s  t h a t  w e  h a v e  n o t  ‘ m a d e ’  Cage
retroactive to cases on collateral review.”). Nothing in
AEDPA suggests that this Court should alter its own
“new rule” and retroactivity analyses, and this Court has
continued to apply that test. See Tyler , 533 U.S.  at 665
(“Under Teague, a new rule can be retroactive to cases
on collateral review if, and on ly if, it falls within one of
two narrow exceptions to  the general rule of
nonretroactivity.”).

3 Citing Learning Res., Inc. v. Trump , 607 U.S. 229, 248–49 (2026),
Johnson contends that “[w]here  Congress intends to adopt a
judicially crafted or specialized meaning, it does so ‘expressly.’”
Resp. Br. 26. The relevant portion of the opinion states that “this
Court sometimes assumes that Congress incorporates judicial
definitions into legislation . . . when the term’s meaning was wellsettled before the adoption,” 607 U.S. at 252 (internal quotation
omitted), which “new rule” was in the retroactivity context.
Bostock v. Clayton County,  590 U.S. 644, 658–59 (2020),  which
Johnson also cites for this proposition, Resp. Br. 26, does not discuss
legislation incorporating judicial definitions.

11

5. Johnson suggests that un der AEDPA, “new rule”
depends solely on “the novelty (or lack thereof) of the
rule itself,” Resp. Br. 23,  regardless of when the
defendant’s conviction became final. As the United
States explains, this interpr etation renders “new rule”
close to meaningless. See U.S. Amicus Br. 23 (“The word
‘new’ would mean next to nothing under such an
approach.”). Every argument is, presumably, based on a
rule that was, at some time, “new.”
Nor is Johnson’s argument consistent with the
requirement that the rule have been “made retroactive
to cases on collateral review.” Such a requirement makes
sense only if the rule is be ing applied retroactively, i.e.,
if it was announced after th e prisoner’s conviction
became final on direct a ppeal. State Amicus Br. 8.
Johnson notes that the statute does not expressly
“say ‘new as to the petitioner,’” Resp. Br. 26, but neither
does it say “previously unavailable to the petitioner.”
Johnson acknowledges that “previously unavailable”
necessarily refers to the rule’s availability to the
petitioner. See Resp. Br. 13 (“availabili ty is relational”).
In the same way, “new rule” refers to a rule that is “new”
with respect to the petitioner. And  nothing in the text of
§  2 2 4 4 ( b ) ( 2 ) ( A )  i n d i c a t e s  a n  i n t e n t  t o  d e p a r t  f r o m
Teague’s retroactivity test: “[A] case announces a new
rule if the result was not dictated by precedent existing
at the time the defendant’s co nviction became final.” 489
U.S. at 301 (plurality op.); see also 28 U.S.C.
§ 2244(d)(1)(C) (involving a “r ight [that] has been newly
recognized”); Dodd v. United States , 545 U.S. 353, 358–
59 (2005) (“[I]f this Court decides a case recognizing a
new right, a federal prisoner seeking to assert that right

12

will have one year from this Court’s decision within
which to file his § 2255 motion.”).
Interpreting “new rule” and “previously unavailable”
together makes sense: both reinforce that
§ 2244(b)(2)(A) concerns when legal developments
permit prisoners to raise clai ms in second or successive
applications. “Previously unavailable” “refers to the
existence of the ‘new rule of constitutional law,’ not to a
particular prisoner’s  ability to utilize or prevail on it.”
Slusser v. Vereen , 36 F.4th 590, 596 (4th Cir. 2022); see
also Gray-Bey v. United States , 209 F.3d 986, 988 (7th
Cir. 2000) (per curiam) (“[F]o r purposes of [§ 2255(h)(2)]
a rule is ‘unavailable’ until the Supreme Court renders
its decision[.]”); see also Brian R. Means, Federal
Habeas Manual § 11:38 (2026) (“At a minimum,
‘previously’ requires that the new rule be established
after the time of the filing of the prior federal habeas
petition.”).
B. The structure of § 2244( b)(2) confirms the
Director’s interpretation.
The structure of § 2244(b)(2) confirms this
understanding: Section 2244(b)(2 )(A) allows claims to be
asserted in second or succe ssive applications based on
certain legal developments, and § 2244(b)(2)(B) allows
claims based on certain fa ctual developments. As the
United States explains (at 18 –19), this structure is found
throughout AEDPA, including in the limitations period
of § 2244(d).
1. Johnson contends that “[t]he phrase ‘relies on’ does
not mean ‘relies exclusively on,’ and subparagraph (A)—
unlike subparagraph (B)—does not ask courts to
examine whether the facts un derpinning the claim are

13

new or old.” Resp. Br. 20. This is true, but it does not
support Johnson. Section 2244(b)(2)(A) requires a
previously unavailable rule, and “whether the facts
underpinning the claim are new or old” is irrelevant to
whether a rule was previously available.
The Director does not contend that § 2244(b)(2)(B)
bars Johnson’s Atkins claim because the claim involves a
new factual predicate. Se ction 2244(b)(2) generally
prohibits new claims in second or successive
applications. Section 2244(b)(2)(A) is an exception that
Johnson cannot take advantage of because his claim
relies on a new factual pred icate and not a previously
unavailable rule.
Like § 2244(b)(2) and § 2255(h), the limitations
provision contains different paths for legal and factual
developments. See 28 U.S.C. § 2244(d)(1)(C) (“the date
on which the constitutional right asserted was initially
recognized by the Supreme Court, if the right has been
newly recognized by the Supreme Court and made
retroactively applicable to cases on collateral review”);
id. § 2244(d)(1)(D) (“the da te on which the factual
predicate of the claim or cl aims presented could have
been discovered through the ex ercise of due diligence”).
AEDPA’s structure has a consistent pattern: one
provision for legal developments and another for factual
developments.
2. Factual developments allow new claims to be filed
only if they satisfy the requ irements of § 2244(b)(2)(B).
By providing an express prov ision for newly discovered
factual predicates, Congre ss confirmed that a new
factual predicate does not affect  the availability of a rule
under § 2244(b)(2)(A). Sectio n 2244(b)(2)(B) implicitly

14

limits the circumstances in which new factual predicates
allow claims to be raised: “Congress knew how to provide
for second and successive p etitions based on factual
developments” and chose to al low them only in narrow
circumstances. In re Bowles, 935 F.3d at 1218.
Johnson’s interpretation of § 2244(b)(2)(A)—in which
a missing factual predicate renders a rule unavailable—
nullifies these limits. Although he challenges the
example hypothetical posed by the Director, Resp. Br. 24
(noting that Batson has not been made retroactive by
this Court), Johnson does no t quarrel with the broader
principle: Under his textual arguments, a prisoner who
discovers a new factual pr edicate for a claim could
present the claim in a second or successive application
under § 2244(b)(2)(A) based on  the theory that the claim
relies on a rule that was “previously unavailable.” See
Resp. Br. 12 (“was of no practical use”). This would allow
prisoners to evade § 2244( b)(2)(B)’s requirements,
including that “the facts unde rlying the claim” must be
sufficient to establish that “no reasonable factfinder
would have found the applican t guilty of the underlying
offense.” 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii).
Relying on an unpublished decision, Johnson
suggests that the Fifth Circui t’s § 2244(b)(2)(A) holding
applies only to Atkins claims. Resp. Br. 32 (citing In re
Halprin, 788 F. App’x 941, 944 (5th Cir. 2019) (per
curiam)). But the decision below and In re Cathey phrase
the exception more broadly: “[A] claim must have some
possibility of merit to be considered available.” Pet. App.
5a (quoting In re Cathey , 857 F.3d at 232). And In re
Cathey analogizes the unavailability of an Atkins claim
to a Roper claim being unavailable based on a prisoner’s
incorrect beliefs about his age. 857 F.3d at 232.

15

Nor does Johnson make any attempt to harmonize an
Atkins-only exception with the statute’s text. He argues
that “a rule under which the petitioner’s claim has no
possibility of merit” is unavailable. Resp. Br. 14. This
interpretation of § 2244(b)(2) would extend beyond
Atkins claims and allow any newly meritorious claim to
be raised in a second or successive petition.
Johnson argues that the negative implications of
§ 2244(b)(2)(B) should prevent,  at most, claims involving
“newly discovered evidence go ing to guilt or innocence”
from proceeding under § 224 4(b)(2)(A). Re sp. Br. 20.
Other claims involving a ne w factual predicate, he
suggests, could be raised un der § 2244(b)(2)(A). But this
is the wrong inference. By expressly permitting only
claims based on a factual predicate showing that the
prisoner would not have been found guilty of the
underlying offense, Congress made clear that this was
the only type of new factual predicate that would allow a
claim to be asserted in a se cond or successive petition.
This limit was a conscious choice. Amicus National
Association of Criminal Defe nse Lawyers notes that by
the time AEDPA was enacted,  this Court had already
recognized several constitution al rights that limit only
punishment and are unrelated to guilt for the underlying
offense. NACDL Br. 5–6. Congress nonetheless chose
that new factual predicates would allow a claim in second
or successive applic ations only when, inter alia , the
prisoner would not have been found guilty of the
underlying offense.  28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii).

16

C. Atkins was not “previously unavailable” to
Johnson.
Johnson’s Atkins claim does not rely on “a new rule
of constitutional law . . . that was previously unavailable.”
28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A). Atkins was decided before
Johnson committed his crimes, and its rule has always
been available to him. He relied on Atkins (seeking its
extension) in his initial habeas application. Johnson, 617
F. App’x at 303; App. 178–79.
Rather than a “new rule,”  Johnson relies on a new
factual predicate: his diagnosis of intellectual disability
under the DSM-5. Amicus NACDL correctly recognizes
the nature of Johnson’s claim as involving “a previously
unavailable factual basis for a claim under established
legal principles.” NACDL Br. 16 (explaining that
“scientific advances” may iden tify a new factual basis);
see also id.  at 17 (“[R]ecogniz ing advancements in
scientific and clinical diagnostic tools does not change the
fundamental prohibition on execution of the
intellectually disabled.”). 4
Changes in diagnostic st andards are not uncommon.
One recent petitioner, fo r example, invoked the
American Association on Intellectual and Developmental

4 The NACDL’s analysi s and discussion largely support the
Director. It urges affirmance because, like the decision below, it
incorrectly focuses on the availability of a “claim” rather than the
availability of a “rule.” See NACDL Br. 18 (“[T]he Fifth Circuit
correctly allowed Johnso n to pursue a claim that was previously
unavailable.”); id. (“The Court should affirm the Fifth Circuit, and
hold that a claim is previously unavailable when it had no reasonable
chance of success of prevailing[. ]”). Johnson acknowledges that
“previously unavailable” modifies “rule” rather than “claim.” Resp.
Br. 12.

17

Disabilities’ “publication on  January 11, 2021,” “the
DSM-5-TR’s publication on March 18, 2022,” and the
APA’s issuance of “guide lines in August 2026.” In re
Howard, No. 26-40605, 2026 WL 2 980644, at *2 (5th Cir.
Oct. 5, 2026). Under Johns on’s view, each of these
changes in diagnostic standards might have allowed
prisoners to seek relief under Atkins, no matter how long
ago their crimes were committed. Congress did not
delegate AEDPA’s gatekeep ing function to private
mental health associations, and these diagnostic changes
do not permit new claims in second or successive
applications under § 2244(b)(2).
Johnson’s merits brief su ggests that the DSM-5 is
legal rather than factual, ca lling it “no different from a
change in the legal standard.” Resp. Br. 21. This is
incorrect: his habeas applic ation itself describes the
DSM-5 as part of the factua l predicate for the claim. See
App. 25 (“[T]he factual predic ate for the claim relies on
the publication of the DS M-5[.]”); A pp. 30 (“Mr.
Johnson’s claim hinges on the publication of the DSM-5
to make his claim available.”). A publication by the
American Psychiatric Association is not a change in the
law. Johnson contends that the DSM-5 “uncovered no
previously unknown facts” because “Mr. Johnson’s
intellectual and adaptive characteristics” have not
changed, Resp. Br. 29, but historical facts never change.
Instead, a new factual predicate for a claim is discovered,
and Johnson’s diagnosis under the DSM-5 provided a
factual predicate for an Atkins claim—that Johnson is
allegedly intellectually disabl ed—that did not previously
exist.
Even if the APA’s publicat ion of the DSM-5 were a
“change in the legal standard,” Resp. Br. 21, it would not

18

constitute a “new rule of constitutional law, made
retroactive to cases on collat eral review by the Supreme
Court.” 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)( A). The same is true of
Hall v. Florida, 572 U.S. 701 (2014), and Moore v. Texas,
581 U.S. 1 (2017). Johnson con tends that these decisions
simply “illuminate what Atkins means,” Resp. Br. 29–30,
but this Court has already re jected the argument that
“Moore merely spelled out what was clearly established
by Atkins.” Shoop v. Hill , 586 U.S. 45, 48–49 (2019); see
also Weathers v. Davis , 915 F.3d 1025, 1 027–28 (5th Cir.
2019) (“[I]t cannot be contended that Hall . . . simply
enunciated ‘clearly established Federal law’ made
retroactive as required by AEDPA.”). Neither Hall nor
Moore constitutes a new rule of constitutional law made
retroactive by this Court.
Applying § 2244(b)(2)(A) to Johnson’s Atkins claim is
straightforward. The rule of Atkins has always been
available to him, so he cannot satisfy § 2244(b)(2)(A), and
his newly discovered factual predicate—his diagnosis of
intellectual disability purs uant to the DSM-5—does not
satisfy § 2244(b)(2)(B).
D. The Director has consistently urged the
adoption of the Eleventh  Circuit’s decision in
In re Bowles .
Rather than resolve the circuit split, Johnson
suggests that this Cour t dismiss the writ as
improvidently granted, accusing the Director of
changing positions from th e certified question in the
Fifth Circuit and from the peti tion for writ of certiorari.
In truth, the Director has consistently urged the
Fifth Circuit and this Cour t to adopt the Eleventh
Circuit’s holding from In re Bowles, 935 F.3d at 1210. See

19

ROA.275 (“[A]t least one co urt of appeals has soundly
rejected the Fifth Circuit’s holding that the publication
of the DSM-5 makes a claim newly legally available.”);
ROA.361 (quoting In re Bowles “to assert [the Fifth
Circuit’s] conclusion is erroneous”); ROA.401 (“The
Eleventh Circuit explains it  better and more  succinctly,
in soundly reject[ing] the F ifth Circuit’s holding[.]”);
ROA.432 (Johnson: “The Director would have this Court
overrule the Fifth Circui t and follow the Eleventh
Circuit’s opinion in In re Bowles . . . instead.”); ROA.509–
16 (relying on In re Bowles).
The certified question in the Fifth Circuit—
“[w]hether there can be judici ally created exceptions to
[§ 2244(b)(2)],” Pet. App. 8a—reflected the district
court’s understanding that In re Cathey adopted a
“judicially created exception”  to AEDPA. Pet. App. 25a
(district court describing the Fifth Circuit as “read[ing]
a futility exception into sectio n 2244(b)(2)( A)”). The
Director explained the Eleven th Circuit’s disagreement
with the Fifth Circuit in  seeking certification. See
ROA.1090 (“[A]pplying a judicially created futility
exception to § 2244(b)(2)(A) is an issue over which the
Fifth and Eleventh Circuits disagree[.]”); see also
ROA.1109 (Johnson: “The Director’s reliance on In re
Bowles . . .”); ROA.1115 (“[T]wo circuit courts disagree
on the exact question presented by the Director[.]”). The
Director’s appellant’s brief urged the Fifth Circuit to
follow In re Bowles, 935 F.3d at 1210. See Appellant’s Br.
28–29, 31, 34. And the Fifth Circuit panel understood the
certified question in this co ntext: “[W]e understand the
parties’ question more accu rately to be this: Whether
‘previously unavailable’ can be read in the way Cathey
instructs[?]” Pet. App. 6a. The panel, “[i]n answer to that

20

question . . . affirm[ed] [its] interpretation of ‘previously
unavailable’ in Cathey as the correct interpretation.” Id.
The issue was raised and decided below.
Nor is there any conflict between the petition for writ
of certiorari and the Director’s  merits brief. The petition
explains the circuit split an d that “[t]he Eleventh and
Fourth Circuits hold that whether a claim would have
been meritorious does not a ffect whether the rule was
previously available.” Pet. i. The Director has
consistently urged this Court to adopt the Eleventh
Circuit’s rule from In re Bowles . Compare Pet. 2
(arguing that “‘previously un available’ does not depend
on ‘whether the claim would have been a winning one at
the time of the first petition,’ only on ‘whether it would
have been feasible for the petitioner to bring the claim
then’” (quoting In re Bowles, 935 F.3d at 1218–19)), with
Opening Br. 21 (“Whether a rule was ‘previously
unavailable’ depends on ‘whether the petitioner could
have relied on [a] ‘new rule’ in his initial habeas petition,’
not ‘whether the claim would have been a winning one at
the time of the first petition.’” (quoting In re Bowles, 935
F.3d at 1218–19)). Johnson cr iticizes the modification of
the question presented from a rule’s availability when a
petitioner “could have assert ed a claim based on the rule
in a prior federal habeas peti tion” to availability “when
this Court announced the rule before the filing of the
prisoner’s prior federal ha beas petition,” but the
Director’s position is that the two are substantively
identical. If this Court anno unced a rule before the prior
federal habeas petition, then  the prisoner necessarily
“could have relied on [it] in his initial habeas petition.” In
re Bowles , 935 F.3d at 1218; see also Pet. 19
(“[C]onstitutional rules that were established at the time

21

of the applicant’s last [fed eral proceeding] were not
‘previously unavailable[.]’” (quoting In re Williams , 364
F.3d 235, 239 (4th Cir. 2004))).
Throughout this case, the Director has consistently
argued that the Fift h Circuit erred in In re Cathey  and
that the Eleventh Circuit’s holding in In re Bowles
should be followed instead. As this Court recognized in
granting the petition for writ  of certiorari, this split
warrants resolution by th is Court, and under the
Eleventh Circuit’s rule, the motion to dismiss should
have been granted.
II. AEDPA Limits Second or Successive Petitions.
Johnson relies on the intuit ion that he should receive
a single bite at the apple for his Atkins claim. Resp. Br.
16 (“Congress meant to restrict petitions filed by
prisoners who had a full and fair opportunity to present
a claim and squandered it or strategically held it in
reserve.”). Johnson embraces the abuse of the writ
comparison, Resp. Br. 16,  arguing in effect that he
should be permitted to rais e his claim now because he
“has a legitimate excuse for fa iling to raise” it earlier.
McCleskey v. Zant, 499 U.S. 467, 490 (1991).
But AEDPA changed the la w by placing “added
restrictions” on second or successive habeas petitions.
Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651, 664 (1996); see also Jones,
599 U.S. at 476 (“AEDPA st rictly limited ‘second or
successive’ § 2255 motions.”).
Johnson is incorrect to char acterize the Director as
suggesting that he should  have filed a frivolous Atkins
claim in his initial federal ha beas application. Resp. Br.
18 (citing Panetti v. Quarterman , 551 U.S. 930 (2007)).
Johnson did not forfeit a viable Atkins claim because of

22

a procedural misstep. His claim is unavailable because of
the balance struck by Co ngress between finality and
error correction. AEDPA’s limits mean that some claims
cannot be raised, and changes in diagnostic standards do
not allow an Atkins c l a i m  t o  b e  r a i s e d  i n  s e c o n d  o r
successive applications.
AEDPA reflects “Congress’  judgment regarding the
central policy question of postconviction remedies—the
appropriate balance between finality and error
correction.” Jones, 599 U.S. at 491. In this case, where
Johnson discovered a new fa ctual predicate for a claim
unrelated to his guilt for the underlying offense, 28
U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B), Cong ress chose “finality over
error correction.” Jones, 599 U.S. at 480. 5
As the amicus briefs confirm, Congress had strong
policy reasons for making such a choice. See State
Amicus Br. 2 (detailing th e “profound injury to the
powerful and legitimate interest in punishing the
guilty”); Opening Br. 37–39. And the absence of finality
imposes ongoing harm on victims, who must wait for
years (even decades) before knowing whether a capital
sentence will be carried out. Aparece Amicus Br. 15.
Johnson committed his crimes more than twenty
years ago. “One of the law’s ve ry objects is the finality of
its judgments.” McCleskey, 499 U.S. at 491. AEDPA
bars Johnson from raising an Atkins claim in his second
federal habeas application.

5 Welch v. United States , 578 U.S. 120 (2016), discusses finality
interests in determining whether rules should be made retroactive
and applied in an initial § 2255 motion, id. at 131, not whether
AEDPA permits the filing of a second or successive petition.

23

CONCLUSION
For these reasons, this Court should correct the Fifth
Circuit’s interpretation of § 2244(b)(2)(A) and reverse
the judgment below.
